pass_a_gloss: [...] for [while he holds] us into the spiritual strength of the God over all, we keep safe in ourselves the bright beauty of our own nature. But he removing the help, we will surely be bare of every good, and having cast off the fairness of the glories from virtue, we will be subject to the passions of dishonour, and we will serve enemies. [Lemma, Isaiah 4:1:] And seven women will take hold of one man, saying: Our bread we will eat, and our garments we will put around us, only let your name be called upon us, take away our reproach. Having very well completed the account upon the women of the Jews going from luxury and wealth into captivity, he tries to show that the cities of Judaea will remain empty of men, and will be in much scarcity of those of old most warlike. For he said that, All your strong ones will fall by sword. What sort then is the showing of what I said? Very cleverly and elegantly prepared. For the law through Moses saying to the sons of Israel: There will not be in you one without offspring nor barren; among the last reproaches it had been reckoned among the Jews for a woman not to give birth, or for any of those counted among men to be without offspring. For at once the blame of the offspringless and barren was rubbed upon them. And the law was spiritual. For the God of all was promising that the spiritual Israel, that is, mind seeing God, will not be fruitless, nor made barren, but rather fruitful and as some land fine and choice. But the Jews were understanding fleshly; for they were soul-men, not having spirit. There will be then, he says, so great a scarcity of males throughout the country, the war having consumed the race, that seven women, or many, take hold of one man and say: Our bread we will eat, and our garment we will put around us; only let your name be called upon us, take away our reproach. Do you see how they fear the reproach of childlessness, and refuse very much the name of the offspringless and barren? For they come not seeking the customary things, and as many things as it is custom for women to receive from those dwelling with them; for they say they will suffice for themselves toward this, but ask only, as I said, the taking away of the reproach. Look then at the depth of the word. For if the one called upon were rich, the women would not have said: Our bread we will eat, and our garment we will put around us. But since they know that those saved from the war and having scarcely escaped have fallen into last poverty, and have much wretchedness, they seek wholly nothing from them, but ask only to become mothers of children. And the account of the history is in these. But they carry the thing set before us [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … us in the spiritual strength of God who is over all, we keep safe in ourselves the bright beauty of our own nature. But when he withdraws his help, we shall be utterly stripped of every good; having lost the beauty of the glories that come from virtue, we shall be subject to dishonorable passions (Romans 1:26) and shall be slaves to enemies.
“And seven women will take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach” (Isaiah 4:1).

Having fully completed his account of the Jewish women who would go from luxury and wealth into captivity, he tries to show that the cities of Judea will be left empty of men, and will have a great scarcity of those who were once the finest fighters. For he had said, “All your strong men will fall by the sword” (Isaiah 3:25).

What, then, is the proof of what I have said? It is framed with great skill and elegance. The law given through Moses says to the sons of Israel, “There shall be no one childless or barren among you” (Deuteronomy 7:14). So among the Jews it was counted one of the worst reproaches for a woman not to bear children, or for any man to be childless; for at once the stigma of the childless and the barren was fastened on them.

The law was indeed spiritual (Romans 7:14). For the God of all was promising that the spiritual Israel, that is, the mind that sees God, would not be fruitless or made barren, but fruitful instead, like a good and choice land. But the Jews understood it in a fleshly way, for they were natural men, not having the Spirit (Jude 19).

So, he says, there will be such a scarcity of males in the land, once the war has consumed the race, that seven women, that is, many, will take hold of one man and say: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach.” Do you see how they dread the reproach of childlessness, and how strongly they refuse the name of childless and barren? For they come not seeking the usual things, what wives are accustomed to receive from their husbands; they say they will provide for themselves in this, and ask only, as I said, that their reproach be taken away.

Note the depth of the passage. If the man they appealed to had been rich, the women would not have said, “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing.” But since they know that those who were saved from the war and barely escaped have fallen into utter poverty and great misery, they ask nothing at all of them, and seek only to become mothers of children.
That is the sense of the history. But they carry the passage before us over …
